summary: Commander is a command-line argument parser in six files. lib holds the whole library: Command, Option, Argument, Help, errors and did-you-mean suggestions. Everything else is verification and explanation, with 133 test files, 45 runnable examples, long-form docs including a Chinese translation, and hand-written TypeScript typings that are themselves type-tested.

districts.purpose: The entire library: the command tree, options, arguments, help rendering, error types and similar-name suggestions.

districts.name: Proving Grounds
districts.purpose: One test file per behaviour, named after the feature it pins, plus fixture programs for subcommand execution.

importantModules.role: The Command class: subcommands, parsing, action handlers, hooks and the program lifecycle. Almost the whole library.
Option definitions: flags, negation, variadic values, defaults, presets, choices and environment variable sources.
Positional arguments: required and optional names taken from the angle or square brackets, variadic form, defaults, choices and custom parsing.
Help text generation: layout, wrapping, sorting and the hooks that let a program override any of it.
CommanderError and InvalidArgumentError, the typed failures a program can catch instead of exiting.
Edit-distance matching behind the did-you-mean line printed after an unknown option or command.
The entry point: exports the default program, the Command, Option, Argument and Help classes, the error types and the createX helpers.
The TypeScript surface, maintained by hand against the JavaScript implementation.
tsd type tests over the declarations, run by npm test alongside the behaviour suite.
An ESM package with no runtime dependencies: npm test runs node --test and the TypeScript check, and only index.js, lib and typings ship.
The main documentation: quick start, options, commands and command-arguments, action handlers, hooks, help and parsing configuration.
The parsing life cycle written out step by step, from options and environment variables down to the leaf command, and where each hook fires.
The awkward cases the readme skips: options taking varying numbers of option-arguments, and the parsing ambiguity they create.
How to reshape the built-in help through configureHelp or a Help subclass: data properties, styling and layout.
Defines the four words the rest of the documentation relies on: option, option-argument, command and command-argument.
The features that still work but should not be used in new code, such as the RegExp option parameter and the --help event listeners.
Semantic versioning with a major release roughly every six months, timed to Node.js LTS end-of-life, and what older lines still receive.
createTestCommand: a Command with exitOverride set and output suppressed, so tests see exceptions instead of process.exit.
The fixture program the executable-subcommand tests spawn, declaring install, search, cache, echo, listen and a hidden default command.
Subcommands implemented as stand-alone executables: pm declares install, search and update, which run as separate pm-* files.
A program with a global --config option and setup and exec subcommands that each add options and an action handler.
The quick start program from the readme: one argument, a --separator option and a --first flag.
The boolean and value options example, including the negatable --no-cheese form paired with --cheese <type>.
The Chinese translation of options-in-depth.md: options taking a variable number of arguments, the parsing ambiguity that creates, and combined short options.
The Chinese translation of deprecated.md: the RegExp option parameter, noHelp, the global Command default import and the --help event listeners.
Flat config layering the eslint recommended rules, typescript-eslint with separate setups for the JavaScript and TypeScript files, and prettier.
The shared TypeScript settings, with checkJs on so the JSDoc in lib is type-checked; tsconfig.js.json and tsconfig.ts.json narrow it per language.
Keep a Changelog history of every release, including the 15.0.0 move to ESM only and its migration tips.
How the project takes issues and pull requests, including that pull requests go against the develop branch.
The Chinese translation of the readme, maintained alongside a partial Chinese copy of the docs directory.

strengths: The library is six small files with one clear responsibility each, which is rare for a parser used this widely.
Tests are named after behaviour (options.variadic, options.required, useColor), so the suite reads as a specification.
Every feature has a runnable example, which makes the documentation checkable rather than merely written.
The hand-written typings carry their own type tests, so the TypeScript surface cannot drift silently.
A published release policy and a deprecations document set expectations for breaking changes.
concerns: lib/command.js carries most of the library, so nearly every change lands in the same file.
The typings are maintained separately from the JavaScript, which is a manual synchronisation step on every API change.
Documentation exists in three places at once: the readme, docs and the examples directory, with the Chinese translation to keep in step as well.
